The archive that remembers

Every civilization writes down what it cannot afford to forget, and then forgets what it wrote. The claim sounds paradoxical, but the pattern is old: archives promise permanence, and deliver it exactly as far as their custodians are funded to deliver it.

The digital archive was supposed to end this. Storage is cheap, copies are free, and forgetting now looks like a choice rather than a fate. That is the promise this essay wants to test — because the ledger underneath it is less kind than the metaphor.

Three shelves

Start with the census. The 1871 United Kingdom census survives in the enumerators' books almost intact — a reminder that paper, kept dry, is a very good archive. The same census, however, records counts that later historians have had to reconstruct, because the published abstracts were themselves compiled under a budget, and the corners that got cut became permanent. The archive remembered what it was paid to remember.

Now the 1990s web. The Internet Archive's crawls preserved a slice of it, and the slice is impressive — but the slice is a slice. Links in papers published in the last two decades now resolve to nothing at a rate measured in the tens of percent, depending on the venue. The dead link is the digital archive's missing shelf: not a fire, not a flood, just a hosting bill nobody paid.

The earlier version of this essay claimed that "the 1871 census recorded 3.1 million households in Scotland." It does not — the recorded figure is about 560,000 households, and the error survives because citing a confident number is easier than checking one. This version carries the correction rather than the claim; the mistake was instructive, but it was still a mistake.

What remembering costs

The conclusion is not that digital archives fail. They succeed at exactly the thing paper did — they remember what someone keeps paying for. The honest version of the promise is narrower and better: an archive that remembers is not a technology but a budget line, renewed every year, with someone's name on it. The reader who wants the strongest version of this argument should verify the numbers above — the point is that they can.
